title: Never Stop Driving #205: The Fake Manual Gearbox
summary: I’ve broken scores of cars, but I never set out to destroy one on purpose like I did back in 2014. That’s when I handed the keys to a 2014 Porsche 911 Turbo to my colleague Bill Caswell and asked him to do repeated dragstrip launches until either the car broke or he puked. The car […]
body_markdown:
I’ve broken scores of cars, but I never set out to destroy one on purpose like I did back in 2014. That’s when I handed the keys to a[2014 Porsche 911 Turbo](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/porsche/911/2014/2014-porsche-911-turbo?id=aCn1I000000D7VfSAK) to my colleague Bill Caswell and asked him to do repeated dragstrip launches until either the car broke or he puked. The car did not break.


The impetus for that torture test emerged during a meeting with Wolfgang Hatz, who was then running Porsche’s Research and Development office. A new version of the Turbo had come out, part of the 991 generation of the Porsche 911, and it was only available with a robotically shifted[dual-clutch transmission](https://www.hagerty.com/media/maintenance-and-tech/faster-than-us-dual-clutch-transmissions/) called PDK. The manual gearbox from the previous-generation 911 Turbo was gone. Hatz defended this decision by saying that the PDK was better in every respect. One example, he said, was that the clutches were so durable that they were essentially lifetime parts.


Porsche


I was skeptical. The 911 Turbo had all-wheel drive and 560 horsepower, a nightmare recipe for the clutch because it’s the link between the powerhouse motor and four-wheel traction. During my career testing cars for *Car and Driver* and *Popular Mechanics,* I’d smoked many clutches obtaining 0-60 times, so Hatz’s boast was especially interesting. How many sprints from rest could the Turbo and its PDK handle, I asked.


He smirked, let out a characteristic German huff, and said, *Der iz no limit.* But what would happen if I took one to a drag strip and did 50 launches, one after another? “Nothing,” he said, practically beaming.


If true, this durability would be one of the few transmission technology advances I’d ever seen in my career. And definitely noteworthy. When I told Hatz I had an opening on our testing calendar, he called over a PR guy and instructed him to get me a car. A few weeks later I picked up the Turbo in Los Angeles.


YouTube/Road & Track


The potential carnage had to be on film, so I asked Caswell to make a[video documenting the test.](https://youtu.be/A5DRCTW-Q7o?si=g64c_ViDHZDVD43l) Caswell, you might remember, famously burst onto the internet car scene when he[crashed the professional rally circuit with his homebuilt BMW.](https://www.jalopnik.com/how-a-500-craigslist-car-beat-400k-rally-racers-5497042/) (You can catch my recent interview with him[here.](https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/the-racer-who-broke-the-internet-a/id1720205748?i=1000648479202) ) Twelve years ago, we were green when it came to capturing car sounds, so please forgive our production quality. But you’ll see in the video that, indeed, the Porsche performed flawlessly over 50 back-to-back launches. Amazing. (Hatz, by the way, moved to VW and[later spent time in jail for the Dieselgate scandal](https://www.thedrive.com/news/20153/porsches-wolfgang-hatz-father-of-918-spyder-and-919-lmp1-hybrid-is-still-in-jail-over-dieselgate) .)


Ferrari


This trip down memory lane was inspired by my colleague Jason Cammisa’s recent film on the new[Ferrari 12Cilindri Manuale](https://youtu.be/-5vuipaI7l0?si=Dit2REv9zEOLBQ4i) and its fake manual transmission. This version of the 12Cilindri has an automated dual-clutch gearbox like the Porsche Turbo that Caswell and I put through the wringer, but it also has a clutch pedal and manual gear lever that are not connected to anything mechanical. They’re like the units you find in driving simulators.


This new feature brings up all sorts of debate. Enthusiasts love manual transmissions, and vintage cars with stick shifts are often worth multiples more than the same model with automatics. People like me bemoan the fact that there are precious few new cars on the market today that are available with manual transmissions. Even the Corvette dropped the manual. The fact is, however, that new car buyers overwhelmingly opt for automatics and the cost of engineering both manual and automatic transmissions is simply too high for most manufacturers. Is the fake real enough or just a parlor trick?


YouTube/Hagerty


Cammisa handles this debate in his usual thoughtful and fully baked way. He traces the history of automotive transmissions and reminds us how rarely drivetrain tech makes a leap forward. Ferrari’s fake manual is one of them, according to Cammisa, and he considers the simulation to be incredibly close to the real thing.


It’s not perfect, but the Ferrari system does offer the benefits of the dual-clutch automatic with the involvement of selecting gears yourself. If the system makes driving more fun, I’m all for it. After all, every modern gas pedal is also a simulation, since manufacturers ditched mechanical throttle cables years ago.


If there’s a rub, it’s the price: About $200,000 for the Ferrari fake manual option. Consider, however, that dual-clutch gearboxes debuted on expensive cars but have trickled down to other cars—even my daughter’s humble $25K VW Jetta has one. I cautiously hope we’ll see many more fake manuals, at affordable prices, in more cars soon. After all, the more folks enjoy driving, the less inclined they’ll be to hand over the controls to a Waymo robot.
